draft.title: Wellbeing in cities, regions and remote Australia
card: Wellbeing in Australia is generally high, but it is not the same everywhere. On average, people in capital cities, such as Melbourne, have higher wellbeing than people in many remote and regional areas.
Remote areas often have lower average incomes and fewer jobs. Some regional towns do too. There are also often fewer services, such as hospitals, specialist doctors and schools.
Distance matters. A person in a remote or regional town may travel hundreds of kilometres for specialist care or for further study, such as TAFE or university.
On average, people in remote areas live shorter lives than people in capital cities. Lower incomes and harder access to services help explain this gap, though it does not apply to every person.
draft.remember: On average, remote and some regional areas often have lower incomes, fewer services and shorter lives than capital cities.

a.q: Why is wellbeing often lower in some remote and regional areas than in capital cities?
opts: Lower incomes and fewer services, often far away
Higher incomes, but fewer people to share them with
More services, but each one costs more to use
Shorter lives, which then cause lower incomes
a.why: Remote and some regional areas often have lower incomes, fewer jobs and fewer services, and long distances make services harder to reach. The option about shorter lives reverses cause and effect: lower incomes and poor access help explain shorter lives, not the other way round.
a.clue: Check how the card compares incomes and services outside capital cities.

b.q: Tom lives on a cattle station in outback Western Australia. Compared with someone living in Melbourne, what is Tom more likely to experience?
opts: A long trip to see a specialist doctor
A higher average income than in Melbourne
A wider choice of schools close to home
A longer expected life than in Melbourne
b.why: Remote areas often have fewer services spread over long distances, so seeing a specialist can mean a long trip. Remote areas tend to have lower incomes, fewer schools and shorter lives on average, so the other options describe the opposite of the usual pattern.
b.clue: Recall how remote areas compare with capital cities on income, services and life span.

a.best: Lower incomes and fewer services, often far away

b.best: A long trip to see a specialist doctor
